prime.problem: Picking index i with probability w[i] / sum(w) by prefix sums and binary search costs O(log n) per draw, about 20 comparisons at n = 10⁶; repeating each index w[i] times makes a pick O(1) but costs sum(w) memory. For many draws from fixed weights there is an O(1)-per-pick table of only n columns.
prime.fits: Sixth maths card. It is a precomputation trade like the factorial tables on the modular card: pay O(n) once, then answer each query in O(1). It connects to the random-pick structures in course 1.
expect: scaling by n so the average column is full
keep height and alias per column
why the build never gets stuck
prime.goal: Build an alias table by hand, prove each index keeps its total height, and pick with one uniform column plus one biased coin.

attend: Why scale each weight by n, and what does that make the average column height?
Why does each build step finish exactly one column for good?
Why can a short column always find a tall one to fill it from?
Why does P(i) come out as w[i] / T after the heights are moved around?
When does the O(n) rebuild make a Fenwick tree the better choice?

must: Scale heights to n·w[i] → they average exactly T = sum(w) → a short column (< T) pairs with a tall one → the tall one tops it up → every column ends exactly T tall with at most two indexes
Building only moves height between columns → index i keeps total height n·w[i] → P(i) = (1/n)·Σ h<sub>c</sub>(i)/T = w[i]/T
Remaining heights always average T → if any is short, another is tall → the loop never gets stuck; integer scaling means no rounding leftovers

O(n) build once → each pick is one uniform column + one comparison → O(1), independent of n; but any weight change forces an O(n) rebuild → Fenwick prefix sums for changing weights (O(log n) update and pick)
elevated: An integer coin randrange(T) < keep makes each column's split exactly keep/T → a float uniform coin is only approximately right

compress.prompt: From memory, build the table for w = [1, 3, 2, 4] (heights 4, 12, 8, 16, T = 10), writing each step's column and the leftover height, and show P(3) = 0.4 from the columns.

retrieve.q: Explain why the alias table gives exactly the right probabilities, even though index 3's height is split across three columns.
answer: each column is chosen with probability 1/n
within a column, i is chosen with probability (its height there)/T
summing over columns gives (total height of i)/(n·T) = n·w[i]/(n·T) = w[i]/T

retrieve.q: Walk through step 2 of the card's build: which indexes are popped, what column is made, and where the large index goes.
answer: 3's height drops to 14 − 6 = 8 < 10, so it goes onto the small stack

retrieve.q: Fixed weights with 10⁷ draws, weights that change every draw, and a handful of draws: pick a sampler for each.
answer: 10⁷ draws, fixed: alias, O(1) per pick after O(n) build
changing weights: Fenwick tree prefix sums, O(log n) update and pick
a few draws: random.choices, one line (O(log n) per pick is irrelevant)

compare.q: Both make a uniform-looking random choice correct for a skewed target. What does each precompute, and what does each pick cost?
answer: random pick with blacklist remaps blacklisted slots to valid ones: a uniform draw plus one lookup
alias moves probability mass so every column is full: a uniform column plus one coin
both: O(n) or O(blacklist) setup, O(1) per pick

compare.q: Prefix sums + bisect is the usual weighted pick. What does the alias method give up to get O(1) picks, and when does prefix-sum win anyway?
answer: alias gives up cheap updates: any change rebuilds the table
prefix sums: O(log n) per pick, but with a Fenwick tree updates are O(log n) too
for few draws or changing weights, prefix sums are simpler and fast enough

predict.q: Build the table for w = [1, 1, 1, 5] in your head. Predict how many of the 4 columns contain index 3, and check P(3) = 5/8 from them.
predict.answer: All 4. Heights are 4, 4, 4, 20 with T = 8: index 3 tops up each of the three short columns by 4 and keeps a full column of 8 for itself. P(3) = (1/4)·(4/8 + 4/8 + 4/8 + 8/8) = (1/4)·2.5 = 0.625 = 5/8.

apply.task: Build the alias table for w = [2, 1, 1] by hand, following the card's stack order (pop from the end of each list). Write each column as (keep, low, alias), then compute P(0) from the columns and check it against 2/4.
apply.hint: Index 0 starts large at 6, drops to 5 after the first column and to 4 after the second, which is exactly full.
